clinicalPearls: A rare autoimmune overlap disorder combining features of lichen planus and bullous pemphigoid, in which tense subepidermal blisters arise both on lichenoid papules and on clinically normal-appearing skin.
Blistering on uninvolved skin is a key clue distinguishing it from bullous lichen planus, where blisters form only within pre-existing lichenoid lesions.
Typically the lichenoid eruption appears first and blistering follows, often favouring the limbs; mucosal and nail involvement can occur.
Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone, as in bullous pemphigoid, distinct from the fibrinogen band and cytoid bodies of lichen planus alone.
Circulating antibodies target the BP180 (collagen XVII) antigen, characteristically the C-terminal portion of the NC16A domain, differing from classic bullous pemphigoid epitope patterns.
Can be triggered by drugs (including certain antihypertensives, antibiotics and biologic/checkpoint agents), phototherapy and, rarely, underlying malignancy.
Salt-split skin immunofluorescence localises immunoreactants to the epidermal (roof) side, supporting a BP180-directed process.
Tends to be more responsive to therapy and to affect younger patients than classic bullous pemphigoid; topical and systemic corticosteroids with steroid-sparing agents are mainstays.
reference.pathophysiology: Lichen planus pemphigoides is understood as a two-step autoimmune phenomenon. A T-cell-mediated lichenoid interface reaction, as in lichen planus, damages basal keratinocytes and the dermo-epidermal junction; this inflammatory injury is thought to expose or release hemidesmosomal basement-membrane antigens that are normally sequestered, a form of epitope spreading. The immune system then generates autoantibodies against BP180 (type XVII collagen), particularly epitopes within and adjacent to the NC16A domain, producing a bullous-pemphigoid-like humoral response. Binding of these IgG autoantibodies, with complement activation and recruitment of eosinophils and neutrophils, disrupts the hemidesmosomal attachment and creates tense subepidermal blisters. Because the antibody response is directed at the basement membrane generally rather than only at inflamed skin, blisters can develop on normal-appearing skin as well as on lichenoid lesions, which is the defining clinical and immunopathological distinction from bullous lichen planus.
additionalDifferentials: Bullous lichen planus (blisters confined to lichenoid lesions only)
Erythema multiforme and other subepidermal blistering disorders
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy of a lichenoid lesion and of a blister edge for routine histology
Direct immunofluorescence showing linear IgG and C3 at the basement membrane zone
Indirect immunofluorescence and salt-split skin to localise antibodies to the blister roof
Serum BP180 (NC16A) enzyme immunoassay for circulating autoantibodies
Detailed drug history including antihypertensives, antibiotics and checkpoint inhibitors
Age-appropriate malignancy screening where clinically indicated
redFlags: Rapidly extending blistering with widespread skin denudation and risk of fluid loss or secondary infection
Mucosal involvement compromising oral intake or vision
New onset following a checkpoint inhibitor, suggesting an immune-related adverse event needing oncology input
Features suggesting underlying malignancy or paraneoplastic pemphigus
reference.prognosis: Lichen planus pemphigoides generally carries a better prognosis than classic bullous pemphigoid, often responding well to corticosteroids and steroid-sparing therapy with sustained remission. Drug-induced cases typically settle after the trigger is withdrawn.
pitfalls: Mislabelling it as bullous lichen planus and missing the basement-membrane autoantibody process
Failing to biopsy normal-appearing perilesional skin for direct immunofluorescence
Overlooking a drug or checkpoint-inhibitor trigger
Assuming the same therapeutic intensity and prognosis as classic bullous pemphigoid
Not distinguishing the epidermal-side (roof) binding on salt-split skin from dermal-side patterns
